sections.title: Backup Types
sections.content:
Understanding backup types requires understanding two separate operations: the BACKUP operation (writing data to the backup location) and the RESTORE operation (reading data back from it). Every backup type makes a tradeoff between these two.
Full backup: copies all selected data â€” every file, every time a full backup runs. Advantages: every backup is self-contained and complete. Restore requires only one backup set. The fastest restore of any backup type. Disadvantages: the slowest backup operation. Requires the most storage. Running a daily full backup of a large dataset is storage-intensive and time-consuming â€” typically impractical for frequent scheduling.
Incremental backup: the first run is a full backup â€” a baseline. Every subsequent backup captures only the data that changed since the LAST backup of any kind â€” whether that was a full backup or another incremental. Day one: full backup. Day two: only files changed since day one. Day three: only files changed since day two. And so on. Advantages: fastest backup operation of any type. Consumes the least storage per backup session. Disadvantages: slowest restore. To restore to Friday, you need the full backup plus every incremental in sequence â€” Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. If any single incremental in the chain is missing or corrupted, the restore fails at that point. Dependency on the entire chain is the critical weakness of incremental backup.
Differential backup: the first run is a full backup â€” same as incremental. Every subsequent backup captures all data changed since the LAST FULL BACKUP â€” not since the last differential. Day one: full backup. Day two: everything changed since day one. Day three: everything changed since day one â€” including what was in day two's differential. The differential grows larger each day as more changes accumulate. Advantages: restore requires only two sets â€” the full backup and the most recent differential. No chain dependency. If Wednesday's differential is available along with the original full, restore succeeds regardless of what happened to Monday and Tuesday's differentials. Disadvantages: backup size grows throughout the cycle. More storage than incremental per session. Slower backup than incremental as the cycle progresses.
Summary comparison:
- Full: slowest backup, most storage, fastest restore, single set restore
- Incremental: fastest backup, least storage per session, slowest restore, needs full plus ALL incrementals
- Differential: moderate backup speed, moderate storage, moderate restore speed, needs full plus latest differential only
Synthetic full backup: a full backup created by combining a previous full backup with subsequent incremental backups â€” without re-reading the source data on the production system. The backup software assembles the synthetic full from existing backup data. Reduces the backup window impact on production systems while maintaining a complete backup set for fast restore.
---
exam_tips: The exam presents scenarios: "You need the fastest backup with acceptable restore time" = Incremental. "You need the fastest restore" = Full. "You need to restore to Friday â€” what do you need?" = For incremental: full + Mon/Tue/Wed/Thu/Fri. For differential: full + Friday's differential only. Know the restore dependency chain for each type â€” this is the most common exam trap.

sections.title: The 3-2-1 Backup Rule
sections.content:
The 3-2-1 rule is the foundational backup strategy for the exam and for real-world implementation. Three numbers. Three requirements. All three must be satisfied.
3 â€” three copies of data total. The production data counts as copy one. Two backup copies must exist. One backup copy is insufficient â€” backup media fails, backup jobs fail silently, ransomware targets and encrypts local backup drives. Two backup copies provide redundancy.
2 â€” two different media types. Two copies on identical external hard drives does not satisfy the 2-media requirement. The two backup copies must use different storage media. Examples: one on external hard drive and one on tape. One on external drive and one in cloud storage. One on NAS and one on optical media. The reason: a single failure mode â€” a firmware bug, a power surge, a ransomware variant targeting a specific drive type â€” cannot take out both copies if they use different media.
1 â€” one copy stored offsite. Physically separated from the primary location. A fire, a flood, a theft, a ransomware infection that encrypts every drive connected to the local network â€” none of these scenarios reach an offsite copy. Cloud storage counts as offsite. A drive stored at a different physical location counts as offsite. A drive stored in the same building â€” even a different floor â€” is not offsite.
Ransomware and the 3-2-1 rule: ransomware that encrypts local files can also encrypt external drives connected at the time of infection. The offsite copy â€” disconnected from the network and physically separated â€” is the copy that survives. The 3-2-1 rule is the exam's standard answer when a scenario involves ransomware recovery planning.
---
exam_tips: The 3-2-1 rule is the exam's standard answer for ransomware backup protection. When a scenario asks what backup strategy protects against ransomware or site-level disaster, 3-2-1 is the answer. Cloud storage counts as offsite. Two backups on two identical external drives does NOT satisfy the 2-media-types requirement.

sections.title: Gfs Rotation
sections.content:
GFS â€” Grandfather-Father-Son â€” is a backup rotation scheme that provides rolling recovery points across different time horizons without requiring indefinite storage of every backup set.
Son â€” daily backups: run daily. Retained for one week. The most granular recovery point â€” allows restoration to any day within the past week.
Father â€” weekly backups: run weekly (typically the last full backup of the week). Retained for one month. Allow restoration to any week within the past month, even after daily (Son) backups have been recycled.
Grandfather â€” monthly backups: run monthly. Retained for one year or longer â€” sometimes permanently for compliance. Allow restoration to any month within the past year, even after weekly (Father) backups have been recycled.
GFS balances retention depth with storage cost. Keeping every daily backup indefinitely would require exponentially growing storage. GFS recycles short-term backups while preserving periodic checkpoints. Organizations adjust retention periods based on compliance requirements and recovery objectives.
Recovery objectives â€” two terms relevant to backup planning:
RPO â€” Recovery Point Objective: the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. How old can the restored data be? An RPO of 24 hours means a full day of data loss is acceptable. A shorter RPO requires more frequent backups.
RTO â€” Recovery Time Objective: the maximum acceptable downtime. How long can the system be unavailable during recovery? A short RTO may require local hot standby systems in addition to backups.
---
exam_tips: GFS rotation allows recovery to any point across multiple time horizons without infinite storage growth. Know what each level represents and its retention period. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines how much data loss is acceptable. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines how long downtime is acceptable. These two values drive backup strategy decisions.

sections.title: Recovery Methods
sections.content:
When a restore is required, the recovery location and method matter as much as the backup itself.
In-place recovery: restores data to the original location â€” overwriting the current contents at that location with the backup data. Use case: the original system is intact and the goal is rolling back to a previous state â€” after accidental deletion, after a ransomware attack that encrypted local files, or after a configuration change that caused instability. Risk: if the restore process fails partway through, both the current data and the restored data may be in an inconsistent state. Test restore procedures before relying on in-place recovery in a critical scenario.
Alternative location recovery: restores data to a different location â€” a separate directory, a different drive, or a different system entirely. The current data at the original location is not touched. Use cases: verifying backup integrity before committing to an in-place restore; recovering specific files without restoring the entire backup set; restoring to a test environment; recovering files from a backup taken before a system failure where the original system no longer exists.
Backup testing â€” non-negotiable: a backup that has never been tested cannot be trusted. Backup jobs can fail silently â€” the backup software reports success but the data is unreadable on restore. Backup media can become corrupted over time. Test restore procedures on a documented schedule. Verify that restored data is readable and complete. Time the restore â€” how long does a full recovery actually take? If the actual recovery time is three times longer than the RTO, the backup strategy must change.
Onsite vs offsite â€” both serve distinct purposes: onsite backups (local external drives, NAS, tape library) allow fast recovery with no download latency. A restore from a local NAS is complete in minutes. Offsite backups (cloud, remote tape storage, offsite drive rotation) allow recovery after events that affect the physical location. Neither alone is sufficient. The 3-2-1 rule mandates both.
---
exam_tips: In-place recovery = overwrites the current location. Alternative location = restores to a different location, preserving original. Backup testing should ALWAYS be performed â€” an untested backup cannot be trusted. Test the actual restore process, not just the backup job completion status.

sections.title: Scripting Basics
sections.content:
SCRIPTING BASICS
Scripting automates repetitive tasks. The A+ exam does not require you to write scripts â€” it requires you to identify file types, understand constructs, and recognize what environment variables and comments are.
SCRIPT FILE TYPES.
.bat â€” Windows batch file. Runs in Command Prompt (cmd.exe). Uses DOS-style commands â€” echo, set, if, for, call. Legacy automation for Windows environments. Still widely encountered in enterprise.
.ps1 â€” PowerShell script. Modern Windows automation. Far more capable than batch â€” full object pipeline, .NET integration, remote execution. Requires execution policy to permit running: Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned or Bypass depending on context. Default policy restricts unsigned script execution as a security control.
.vbs â€” VBScript. Windows Script Host execution via cscript.exe (command line) or wscript.exe (GUI). Legacy enterprise tool. Still encountered in older environments and some GPO-deployed automation.
.sh â€” Shell script. Runs via bash or sh on Linux and macOS. The Unix equivalent of a batch file. Begins with a shebang line: #!/bin/bash. Made executable with chmod +x.
.py â€” Python. Cross-platform. Runs with the Python interpreter. Common in IT automation, configuration management, and tooling. No compilation â€” the interpreter executes the script directly.
.js â€” JavaScript. Browser-native, but also runs server-side via Node.js. Less common in pure IT administration but present in web automation and scripting contexts.
ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES.
Environment variables are named values stored by the operating system that scripts reference without hardcoding. Windows examples: %USERNAME% (current user), %COMPUTERNAME% (hostname), %PATH% (executable search path), %TEMP% (temp directory), %APPDATA% (user app data path). Linux examples: $HOME, $USER, $PATH. A login script that maps a drive to \\server\homes\%username% works for every user because %username% resolves to the current user's account name at runtime.
COMMENTS.
Lines in a script that are not executed. Used to explain logic or disable code for testing. In batch: REM or :: before the line. In PowerShell and Python: # before the line. In VBScript: ' before the line. The interpreter or engine skips comment lines entirely.
BASIC CONSTRUCTS.
Variables: store a value for later use. Batch: SET name=value. PowerShell: $name = value. Python: name = value. Variables allow scripts to behave dynamically based on input or system state.
Conditionals â€” IF statements: execute a block only when a condition is true. IF the service is stopped, start it. IF the folder does not exist, create it. Conditionals let scripts react to different situations.
Loops: repeat a block of code. FOR loops iterate over a collection â€” files in a folder, lines in a file, items in a list. WHILE loops run until a condition becomes false. Loops eliminate manual repetition.
Operators: comparison operators evaluate conditions â€” equal (==), not equal (!=), greater than (>), less than (<). Logical operators combine conditions â€” AND (both must be true), OR (either must be true), NOT (inverts the result).
SCRIPTING RISKS AND CONSIDERATIONS.
Scripts automate actions at scale — which means errors also execute at scale. Three risk categories are explicitly tested in Objective 4.8.
Unintentionally introducing malware: a script downloaded from an untrusted source may contain malicious payloads embedded alongside legitimate-looking code. Running an untrusted script with elevated permissions gives that payload full system access. Mitigation: only run scripts from verified sources; review script content before execution; use PowerShell execution policy (RemoteSigned or AllSigned) to require scripts be signed by a trusted publisher before they execute.
Inadvertently changing system settings: scripts that modify registry entries, firewall rules, file permissions, service configurations, or user accounts can destabilize or misconfigure a system if the script contains an error or runs on the wrong machine. A registry modification script with incorrect variable values can break application functionality or prevent the OS from booting. Mitigation: test all scripts in a sandbox or test environment before production deployment; take a system backup or checkpoint before running configuration-changing scripts; implement variable validation and error handling within the script.
Browser or system crashes due to resource mishandling: scripts that open unlimited processes, hold memory in loops without releasing it, or generate excessive file I/O can exhaust system resources and cause application or OS instability. A script that spawns a new child process for each item in a large dataset without cleanup will consume CPU and RAM progressively until the system becomes unresponsive. Mitigation: implement resource limits and process cleanup in script logic; test with representative data volumes before running in production; monitor system resource usage during the first execution of any new automation.
---
exam_tips: The incremental restore chain dependency is the #1 exam trap for backup types. If ANY incremental in the chain between the full backup and the restore point is missing or corrupted, the restore fails at that point. Differential eliminates this risk â€” you only need the full backup and the most recent differential.

sections.title: Remote Access Technologies
sections.content:
REMOTE ACCESS TECHNOLOGIES
Remote access allows technicians to support and manage systems without physical presence. The exam tests protocol, port, use case, and security consideration for each method.
RDP â€” REMOTE DESKTOP PROTOCOL.
Microsoft's built-in remote desktop solution. Port 3389 TCP. Provides a full graphical desktop session on a remote Windows machine. Enabled through System Properties > Remote settings â€” must be explicitly enabled; it is off by default. Access controlled by user account membership in the Remote Desktop Users group. Administrators have access by default when RDP is enabled.
Network Level Authentication â€” NLA: requires users to authenticate before a full desktop session is established. NLA reduces the attack surface because the full desktop environment is not rendered until after authentication succeeds.
Security consideration: RDP on port 3389 exposed directly to the internet is one of the most frequently attacked targets in the wild. Mitigation: restrict RDP to internal network access only, require VPN before RDP connection, or use a Remote Desktop Gateway. NLA should always be enabled.
SSH â€” SECURE SHELL.
Port 22 TCP. Provides encrypted command-line access to Linux, macOS, and network devices. Replaces Telnet â€” which transmitted credentials and data in plain text â€” with an encrypted channel. Authentication methods: password authentication (acceptable) or public key authentication (preferred). In public key authentication, the client holds the private key; the server holds the corresponding public key. The connection is authenticated cryptographically without transmitting a password. OpenSSH is available as an optional feature on Windows 10 and 11.
VNC â€” VIRTUAL NETWORK COMPUTING.
Cross-platform remote desktop using the RFB â€” Remote Framebuffer Protocol. Default port 5900. Provides graphical desktop access to Windows, Linux, and macOS. No native encryption â€” VNC sessions should be tunneled through SSH or a VPN for security. Common implementations: RealVNC, TightVNC, UltraVNC. VNC is frequently used for cross-platform remote support scenarios where RDP is not available.
THIRD-PARTY REMOTE TOOLS.
TeamViewer and AnyDesk are commercial tools commonly used for remote support and unattended access. They route sessions through the vendor's cloud relay infrastructure, bypassing firewall restrictions without requiring port forwarding. This is both the convenience and the risk: any machine with the software installed can be connected to from outside the network.
Security implication: third-party remote tools installed without IT authorization are a persistent access risk. Attackers use them as legitimate-appearing backdoors after compromising a machine. These tools should appear in asset inventory, require IT authorization, and be monitored.
Windows built-in alternatives: Remote Assistance allows a user to invite a technician to view and control their session. Quick Assist (Windows 10/11) is the modern replacement â€” the helper enters a code the user generates, and a screen share or full control session is established.
SCREEN SHARE vs FILE TRANSFER.
Screen share: mirrors or provides control of the remote display. The technician sees and can interact with the remote desktop. File transfer: moves files between the local and remote system. Most remote tools support both, but they are distinct functions. Know which applies to the scenario.
RMM — REMOTE MONITORING AND MANAGEMENT.
RMM platforms are used by managed service providers and enterprise IT departments to monitor and manage endpoints at scale. A lightweight agent installed on each managed device reports hardware inventory, software inventory, patch compliance, performance metrics, and alerts to the central RMM console. Technicians can initiate remote sessions, push software deployments, execute scripts, and manage OS updates across thousands of endpoints from a single interface — without requiring physical access or end-user involvement for routine maintenance. Common platforms: NinjaRMM, ConnectWise Automate, Datto RMM, Kaseya. RMM is the mechanism that allows an MSP to proactively manage a client fleet rather than reacting only when users report problems.
SPICE — SIMPLE PROTOCOL FOR INDEPENDENT COMPUTING ENVIRONMENTS.
SPICE is a remote display protocol used primarily with KVM virtual machines on Linux hosts and open-source virtualization platforms such as oVirt and Red Hat Virtualization. SPICE provides high-performance remote console access with support for audio redirection, clipboard sharing, USB device pass-through, and multi-monitor configurations. It is the standard remote console protocol in Red Hat-based virtualization environments — the role that RDP fills for Windows virtual machines. Default port 5900 (same as VNC, configurable per VM). Not used for general Windows endpoint management; specific to VM console access in Linux virtualization environments.
WinRM — WINDOWS REMOTE MANAGEMENT.
WinRM is Microsoft's implementation of the WS-Management protocol — a SOAP-based standard for remote system management. WinRM is the transport layer that PowerShell remoting relies on. Ports: 5985 for HTTP, 5986 for HTTPS. WinRM must be explicitly enabled on the target system: winrm quickconfig enables the service and configures the required Windows Firewall exception. PowerShell remoting commands — Enter-PSSession for interactive sessions, Invoke-Command for remote script execution — use WinRM as their transport. WinRM enables command-line remote management and automation without establishing a full graphical RDP session, making it efficient for scripted administration and bulk configuration tasks.
---
exam_tips: .ps1 requires execution policy to run â€” default policy blocks unsigned scripts. .sh requires the executable bit set (chmod +x). Know which file extension maps to which execution environment.

sections.title: Ai Basics
sections.content:
AI BASICS
Artificial Intelligence has become part of the IT professional's daily environment. CompTIA added AI to Domain 4 â€” Operational Procedures â€” because technicians are increasingly expected to understand what AI tools do, what risks they introduce, and how responsible use policies govern them in the workplace. This is Objective 4.10.
MACHINE LEARNING.
Machine learning is a subset of AI where a system learns patterns from data rather than following explicitly programmed rules. An ML model is trained on a labeled dataset, then applied to new data to classify inputs, predict outcomes, or detect anomalies. Examples relevant to IT infrastructure: spam filters that learn to identify junk email based on content and header patterns, fraud detection systems that flag transactions deviating from historical norms, and predictive maintenance systems that use sensor telemetry to anticipate hardware failures before they occur.
GENERATIVE AI.
Generative AI is a class of AI that produces new content â€” text, images, code, audio â€” in response to a prompt. Large language models such as GPT-based tools and Claude generate human-readable text by predicting likely continuations based on patterns in training data. These tools assist IT professionals with documentation drafting, scripting, troubleshooting research, and summarizing technical procedures.
A critical operational note: generative AI does not look up answers from a live database. It generates responses based on training data, which means it can produce plausible but incorrect output â€” confidently stated errors are a known failure mode. Verify AI-generated technical procedures against authoritative sources before implementing them in production environments.
PRIVACY AND DATA CONSIDERATIONS.
Sensitive data entered into public AI tools may be retained by the vendor, used for model training, or reviewed by vendor personnel depending on the platform's terms of service. This is a significant workplace concern with direct policy implications.
Data that must not be submitted to AI tools without appropriate enterprise agreements: PII â€” Personally Identifiable Information â€” including names, addresses, and identification numbers; PHI â€” Protected Health Information â€” covered under HIPAA; PCI-DSS-regulated data such as payment card numbers; proprietary business information; and internal credentials or system access details.
Organizations with enterprise AI agreements that provide appropriate data handling guarantees â€” contractual prohibitions on training from enterprise data, data isolation, or dedicated instances â€” may permit AI tool use within those boundaries. Know what your organization's agreement covers before using any AI tool for work tasks involving the data types listed above.
ACCEPTABLE USE POLICY FOR AI.
Many organizations are adding AI-specific language to their acceptable use policies. As an IT professional, you may be responsible for enforcing these policies and educating end users on compliance. AI AUP provisions typically address:
Prohibited data types in AI prompts â€” the categories listed above.
Approved vs unapproved AI tools â€” sanctioned enterprise tools differ from consumer free-tier tools in their data handling.
Documentation and disclosure requirements â€” disclosure when AI-generated content is used in formal outputs or deliverables.
Intellectual property: AI-generated code, documentation, and content may have ambiguous intellectual property status. AI output should be reviewed before use in any situation involving licensing, compliance, or contractual obligations.
AI LIMITATIONS — BIAS.
AI bias occurs when a model produces systematically skewed or discriminatory outputs because the training data itself reflects existing inequalities, underrepresentation, or labeling errors. The model learns the patterns present in the training data — including patterns that should not be generalized.
IT-relevant examples: a résumé screening model trained predominantly on historical hiring data for roles with demographic skew will assign lower scores to qualified candidates from underrepresented groups — not because of their qualifications, but because the training data encoded historical patterns. A facial recognition system trained on datasets with limited diversity will produce higher error rates for underrepresented groups. A predictive maintenance model trained on data from one class of hardware environment may perform poorly on hardware configurations not well-represented in its training set.
The three testable AI limitations for Objective 4.10: Bias (training data skew producing systematically skewed outputs), Hallucinations (confidently stated incorrect information), and Accuracy (AI outputs must be verified against authoritative sources before acting on them). All three are explicitly listed in the objective.
---
exam_tips: Environment variables make scripts portable â€” the same login script maps the correct home folder for every user because %username% resolves at runtime to whoever is logged in.

sections.title: Exam Day Guidance
sections.content:
"Before the outro â€” a few practical notes on the exam itself."
The 220-1202 exam: up to 90 questions, 90 minutes. Passing score: 700 out of 900. Question types: multiple choice, multiple select (read carefully â€” these specify how many answers to choose), performance-based questions (drag-and-drop, simulated interfaces â€” these appear early in the exam).
Performance-based questions: take your best attempt and move on. Do not spend 15 minutes on one PBQ while the clock runs. You can flag and return. If you are stuck, answer your best guess, flag it, and complete the rest of the exam before returning.
Multiple-select questions: read the question for the answer count. "Choose TWO" means choosing three is wrong even if three answers are correct-sounding. These are frequently missed because of careless reading.
Scenario questions: the exam presents a situation and asks what you would do. Eliminate answers that are clearly wrong first. Between two plausible answers, apply the actual procedure â€” not what seems fastest or most convenient. The exam tests that you know the correct sequence, not just the general concept.
Final study priorities: the domains are weighted â€” Operating Systems (28%) and Security (28%) together are more than half the exam. Software Troubleshooting (23%) and Operational Procedures (21%) make up the rest. Know the troubleshooting methodology. Know the order of volatility. Know the malware removal steps in sequence. Know backup type tradeoffs.
---
exam_tips: RDP = port 3389. NLA requires authentication before the full remote session is established â€” reduces attack surface by not loading the full desktop for unauthenticated connections. Always require NLA and restrict RDP access to internal network or VPN.

SSH = port 22, encrypted CLI. Telnet = port 23, plaintext â€” never use Telnet for remote administration. Key-based authentication is stronger than password-based â€” the private key never leaves the client.

VNC has no native encryption â€” must be tunneled. Third-party tools (TeamViewer, AnyDesk) require IT authorization â€” they can be used as backdoors by attackers. Remote Assistance and Quick Assist are the Microsoft-built alternatives that still require user consent.

What remote access technology provides a secure command-line connection to manage remote servers?
What is the difference between RDP and VNC?
options: RDP creates a new session; VNC mirrors the existing active display session
RDP is Linux-only; VNC is Windows-only
VNC is faster than RDP in all cases

practice_questions.q: What remote support tool allows a technician to view and control a user desktop with the user permission?
options: Remote assistance tools (e.g., Quick Assist, TeamViewer, Remote Desktop with consent)

practice_questions.q: What is the purpose of a jump server (or bastion host) in network security?
options: Provide internet access to all users
Distribute IP addresses to remote users
Act as a secure intermediary for administrators to access systems in a protected network segment

practice_questions.q: Which remote desktop configuration must be enabled on the target Windows PC before RDP connections can be made?
options: Remote Desktop must be enabled in System > Remote Desktop settings, and the user must have permission

practice_questions.q: What cloud-based remote access tool built into Windows 11 allows a user to share their screen with another person using a code?
What Windows tool allows an administrator to manage a remote computer through a graphical snap-in console?
options: MMC (Microsoft Management Console) with remote computer connection

practice_questions.q: What security best practice should be implemented when enabling RDP on a workstation or server?
options: Use default port 3389 for easy access
Disable Windows Firewall to allow connections
Restrict access by IP address, use strong passwords, enable NLA, and change the default port
Use a blank administrator password for convenience

practice_questions.q: A technician needs to provide unattended remote support to a branch office server after hours. Which protocol and default port number should be used for native Windows remote desktop access?
practice_questions.explanation: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is the native Windows remote access protocol listening on TCP port 3389 by default. It provides full graphical desktop access to Windows systems and is commonly used for unattended remote server administration.
